newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian Air applauds Ottawa forcing vote.
newsitem.headline: Canadian Air applauds Ottawa forcing vote.

text.p: Canadian Airlines Corp, which on Wednesday started to see its chances of survival slip away without full union support for its restructuring, applauded a government move to force the union's members to vote freely.
"It's a positive step," said Canadian spokeswoman Claudia Cattaneo. "We've said all along that members should decide and the union leadership should allow these people to vote on this proposal."
Canadian Labor Minister Alfonso Gagliano said today he would use his power to force 3,700 Canadian Auto Workers members at Canadian to vote on the company's survival plan.

Gagliano's move came shortly after short a meeting in Ottawa between Canadian chief executive Kevin Benson, CAW president Buzz Hargrove and Canadian Transport Minister David Anderson failed to yield new support from the union
The CAW was the last of six of Canadian's unions to remain opposed to the carrier's survival plan, which includes a call for sliding-scale wage cuts for employees average about five percent.

All unions must be on side for all the restructuring deal's parts to fall into place. Various aspects include federal and provincial government support and a C$48 million a year cut in fees paid to 33 percent owner AMR Corp.
Hargrove had steadfastly refused to call a vote on the plan, saying the CAW's Canadian members had given enough wage concessions in restructurings over the past five years.
In Wednesday's meeting, Hargrove insisted that the federal government contribute another C$8 million to the life-support package in return for a corresponding reduction in employee wage concessions.
Anderson refused to kick in the extra money, which would have increased Ottawa's share of a C$70 million government and employee savings package to 65 percent from the current 55 percent.

In a somber message to employees recorded shortly before Ottawa's move, Benson expressed grave concern over the airline's future and said Hargrove had one day to begin urging his members' support for the survival plan.
"Absent Mr Hargrove changing his mind in the next 24 hours, I'm afraid I'm out of options," he said, imploring workers to look after customers "to the last."

Canadian is striving to win postponement of about C$170 million in debt payments over the next six months from 70 creditors and equipment lessors, a move that is contingent on the plan being in place.
Benson said some of the carrier's suppliers placed it on cash-only payment terms, stretching Canadian's cash reserves to the limit.
